translations.text: The life and account of the Bagratids, our kings of the Georgians: from where they came to this land,
and from what time they have held the kingship of Kartli, which Sumbat son of David wrote. Adam begot Seth.
Seth begot Enos. Enos begot Cainan. Cainan begot Mahalalel. Mahalalel begot Jared. Jared begot Enoch. Enoch begot Methuselah.
Methuselah begot Lamech. Lamech begot Noah. Noah begot Shem. Shem begot Arphaxad. Arphaxad begot Cainan. Cainan begot Shelah.
Shelah begot Eber. Eber begot Peleg. Peleg begot Reu. Reu begot Serug. Serug begot Nahor. Nahor begot Terah.
Terah begot Abram. Abram begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah. Judah begot Perez. Perez begot Hezron.
Hezron begot Ram. Ram begot Amminadab. Amminadab begot Nahshon. Nahshon begot Salmon. Salmon begot Boaz.
Boaz begot Obed. Obed begot Jesse. Jesse begot King David. King David begot Solomon. Solomon begot Rehoboam.
Rehoboam begot Abijah. Abijah begot Asa. Asa begot Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat begot Joram. Joram begot Uzziah. Uzziah begot Jotham.
Jotham begot Ahaz. Ahaz begot Hezekiah. Hezekiah begot Manasseh. Manasseh begot Amon. Amon begot Josiah. Josiah begot Jehoiakim.
Jehoiakim begot Jeconiah. Jeconiah begot Shealtiel. Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel begot Abiud. Abiud begot Eliakim.
Eliakim begot Azor. Azor begot Zadok. Zadok begot Achim. Achim begot Eliud. Eliud begot Eleazar. Eleazar begot Matthan.
Matthan begot Jacob. Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary and the brother of Cleopas. Cleopas begot Naom. Naom begot Sala.
Sala begot Rehoboam. Rehoboam begot Mokhtar. Mokhtar begot Eliakim. Eliakim begot Benjamin. Benjamin begot Jeroboam. Jeroboam
begot Moses. Moses begot Judah. Judah begot Eleazar. Eleazar begot Levi. Levi begot Joram. Joram begot Manasseh. Manasseh begot Jacob.
Jacob begot Micah. Micah begot Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim begot Jeroboam. Jeroboam begot Abraham. Abraham begot Job.
Job begot Ahab. Ahab begot Simeon. Simeon begot Issachar. Issachar begot Abijah. Abijah begot Gad. Gad begot Asher. Asher begot Isaac.
Isaac begot Dan. Dan begot Solomon. Solomon begot seven brothers, whom God gave him in captivity.
And these seven brothers, the sons of this Solomon, Jews who had come out of captivity, came out of the land of Philistia and arrived at Ekeleats, before Queen Rachel, and received baptism from her.
And they remained in the lands of Armenia, and there, to this present day, their children rule in Armenia.
And four of their brothers came to Kartli. One of them, named Guaram, they appointed eristavi (duke), and he is the eristavi of Kartli and the father of the Bagratids.
And these Bagratids of Kartli are the descendants and kin of that Guaram.
His brother, named Sahak, went to Kakheti and became related by marriage to Nerse.
And the other two of these brothers, named Asam and Varazvard, went to Kambechan, and they killed the Persian commander-in-chief and took possession of Kambechan,
and they settled there to live at Khornabuj. And to this time their children rule in it.
But once the kingship of the sons of Gorgasali came to an end, from that time the nobles (aznaurs) held the rule of Kartli, down to these men.
But the nobles' rule of Kartli came to an end because of their evil deeds.
At that time the catholicos in Mtskheta was Svimon-Petre. Mtskheta was growing weak and Tbilisi was being built up; Armazi was shrinking and Kala was growing great.
And the Persians ruled Kartli, Kakheti, Hereti, Armenia (Somkhiti), Siunik and Vaspurakan.
Catholicos Svimon died, and Samoel took his seat as catholicos, the ninth catholicos.
At that time the catholicos in Mtskheta was Samoel. All Kartli gathered together, and they chose Guaram,
of the lineage of David, who had come together with his brothers Asam and Varazvard, whom we mentioned above.

These had come from Ekletsi. Queen Rakael had baptized them. They were seven Jewish brothers who had come as captives from the land of the Philistines, and they were baptized at Ekletsi by the hand of Queen Rakael.
She changed the names of three of them: she named one Mushel, one Bagrat, who is the father of the Bagratids, and one Abgavar.
One she took in as a son-in-law, and two of them she [?] (perhaps 'presented' or 'summoned') to the kings of Armenia.

And these four brothers set out for Kartli, as we mentioned above. They appointed Guaram as eristavi, and the king of the Greeks gave him the rank of kouropalates as an honor and sent him to Mtskheta.
And he laid the foundation of the Church of the Cross, which is at Mtskheta.
And these three brothers went to Kakheti, and Sahak [?] (perhaps 'summoned') Bakur, son of Nerses. Asam and Varazvard went to Kambechovani,
and they turned the people away from Vezan, the eristavi of Bahram Chobin. They killed Vezan and took possession of Kambechovani. At that time the catholicos in Mtskheta was Samoel.
And at this time the inhabitants of Tbilisi began to build a church. All the people built half of it, and a certain woman built the other half.
And the catholicos in Mtskheta was Bartholomew. After this Guaram, his son Stephen ruled as eristavi, and the brother of Demetre [?].

And they were building the Church of the Cross at Mtskheta. At this time Heraclius, king of the Greeks, passed through and came to Tbilisi, and he took up a position directly facing the fortress of Kala.
And the commander of the fortress called out from the fortress across to King Heraclius and said: "You who wear the beard of a goat and have the neck of a young he-goat!"
When King Heraclius heard these words, he grew angry at them, and he read aloud this saying from the book of the prophet Daniel:
"A goat came up from the west and broke the horns of the ram of the east." And the king said: "If it was of me
that this saying was spoken, then for your insolence toward me I will leave you a twofold repayment."
And he left Jibghu the eristavi in Tbilisi to fight against the fortress of Tbilisi, and he himself set out for Baghdad.
And he went to Gardabani, the land of Varaz-Gagel, and camped at the place called Khuzasheni. Heraclius baptized Varaz-Gagel and all his people.
And he began to build a church, which is the most splendid of all churches. Then he went to Berduji and stopped in the heart of the land.
And he set up a stone cross, laid the foundation of the church of the holy Mother of God, and completed its dome.
Then Jibghu took Kala and captured the fortress of Tbilisi, and seized the commander of the fortress.
And he filled his mouth with drachmas, because he had spoken the praise of King Heraclius.
But for his insolence he flayed him and sent his skin to the king at Gardabani, the land of Varaz Gageli.
And from Gardabani the king moved to Lal [?], and summoned the prince of the Metsekevnelni [?], baptized him, and went to Baghdad.

And he took Baghdad, and seized King Khosrow, and made him bring out the Wood of Life, and began to rebuild Jerusalem, and installed Modestus as patriarch, and from there set out back this way, and arrived in the seventh year.
And before his coming the Sioni church of Tbilisi had been completed, but the church of the Cross was still unfinished.
And this King Heraclius sent heralds to Tbilisi, Mtskheta and Ujarma, ordering that all Christians should go into the church,
and that all the magi and fire-worshippers who had still not been baptized should be put to death.
But they did not want to receive baptism; instead they deceitfully mingled with the Christians.
And they put all of them to the sword, and rivers of blood flowed within the churches.
And he purified the faith of Christ our God, and King Heraclius departed to his own kingdom. And the same Stephen the Great ruled Kartli.
The catholicos was Bartholomew II. In his time and after him Adarnase, the son of that Stephen, ruled.
And in his time three catholicoi succeeded one another: John, Babila and Tabor. After this Prince Adarnase died, and in his place his son Stephen took the throne.
And he completed the church of the Cross, and established there the feast of the Cross, and settled in Tbilisi to live.
And the catholicoi were Samuel and Enon. And in his time the land of Kartli
was registered in a census, and the record was taken to Greece. And news came that the race of Hagar had captured Baghdad.
And after this Stephen, his son Guaram the curopalates was eristavi.
And after him came his son Varaz-Bakur, the anthypatos, who converted the people of Gardabani.
And then came Nerse and his sons Philip, Stephen and Adarnase. And his sons were Gurgen the eristavi and Ashot the curopalates.
Now Ashot the curopalates ruled in that land, and his residences were Barda and Tbilisi, and he held the land that lies around them.
And then the power of the Hagarenes grew strong, and they began to hunt for Ashot the curopalates. And Ashot could not resist them, and he fled from them.
And he set out to go to Greece, and with him were his mother and his wife and two sons who were young in age, the elder Adarnase and the next Bagrat.
But he did not yet have his youngest son Guaram. And few of his people were with him: his household, with their wives and children.
They reached the mountain of Javakheti, on the shore of the great lake Paravani, worn out from the journey, and dismounted to rest on the shore of that lake.
When they had eaten bread, they fell asleep for a little while. And as they slept, great Saracen armies caught up with them.
Then God helped Ashot the Curopalates, and gave his small army victory over them, and they slaughtered countless multitudes.
They came out from there and reached the valley of Shavsheti. At that time the valley of Shavsheti was uninhabited, except for a few villages.
For it had been laid waste in the days of Persian rule, when the Deaf One of Baghdad destroyed all the fortresses and overran Shavsheti and the highlands (Ghadoni) as well.
And again, after that, the deadly plague laid waste Shavsheti and Klarjeti, and only a few people were left here and there.
But the remaining inhabitants of Shavsheti received him with joy and love, and he settled there.
And God gave him victory and made him ruler over Shavsheti and Klarjeti.
Some villages he bought with money, and some that were deserted he rebuilt, and Ashot the Curopalates multiplied the villages in those lands.
And God granted it, and his rule was strengthened by the will of the king of the Greeks.
In the forests of Klarjeti this Ashot the Curopalates found a rock called Artanuji, which Vakhtang Gorgasali had formerly built as a fortress;
it had lain in ruins since the time of that Deaf One of Baghdad. Ashot restored it and built it again as a fortress, and below it, in front of it, he built a town.
Inside that fortress he built a church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and made his own tomb in it, and settled in that fortress to live there.
And afterwards he also gained control of the lands as far as the gates of the city of Bardav.
Many times God gave Ashot the Curopalates victory and great glory in battle.
Once Ashot went out to gather an army for war against the Saracens.
He came to a certain place and sent out men to summon the army.
Before his army had gathered to him, the Saracens attacked him unexpectedly and put him to flight.
He set out and reached the valley of Nigali, and began to seek people, so that he might somehow enlarge his army.
Those whom he had summoned set out to come before him, but they were coming to kill him.
Until they reached his door Ashot did not know of their treachery, and only when they reached his door did he perceive what they intended.
He had none of his own people with him except a few. He could not withstand them.
For this reason Ashot the Curopalates fled into a church, and they wounded him with the sword on the altar, and that altar was drenched with his blood,
for they slaughtered him there like a sheep on the steps of the altar, and his spilled blood can still be plainly seen today.
When his people, who were in Doliskana, heard the news that their lord Ashot had been killed by the hands of the sons of Oroz-Moroz,
they left Doliskana and pursued the murderers of their lord. They overtook them at a resting-place on the Chorokhi and cruelly slaughtered them,
until not one of them was left. They carried away the dead Ashot the Curopalates and buried him in his tomb in the fortress of Artanuji, in the church of the holy apostles.
For this Ashot the curopalates was killed in the year 6430 from the beginning [of the world], in the thirteenth cycle of the chronicon, year 46, on the twenty-ninth day of the month of January.
And he left three sons: the eldest, Adarnase, and the next after him, Bagrat. These two
were with him when he came to Shavsheti-Klarjeti. But the youngest, Guaram, was born only after the coming to Artanuji.
And after the death of Ashot, their father, the outer lands that the sons of Ashot held were taken from them by the Saracens, because they were not yet of full age.
But when they came of full age, God gave back to them again all that their father had possessed.
And while they were still under age, they were brought up in the fortress of Artanuji, and all the valleys of Shavsheti, Klarjeti and Nigali paid tribute to the Saracens.
But on this side of Artanuji they took possession of those holdings, the patrimonial estates of their father, and made Bagrat curopalates.
And God prospered their rule. And the sons of their eldest brother, Adarnase son of Ashot, were three:
Gurgen, who was made curopalates in the days of his old age, and his brothers Ashot Kekelai and Sumbat of Artanuji, who in his reign was made anthypatos-patrikios.
And the sons of Bagrat the curopalates were three: David, who was made curopalates after his father, Adarnase, and Ashot.
And the sons of the youngest, Guaram son of Ashot, were two: Nasra and Ashot.
Now Ashot Kekelai, son of Adarnase, died in chronicon year 87, and left Gurgen, who was afterwards made curopalates, and Sumbat of Artanuji the anthypatrikios.
Ashot, son of Guaram the mampali, died before his father, in chronicon year 89. He left no son.
Adarnase, son of Bagrat the curopalates, died in chronicon year 94, while his father was still alive, and he left no child.
And his father, Bagrat the curopalates, son of Ashot the curopalates, died in chronicon year 96, and left sons: David, whom they made curopalates after him;
and he was killed by the hand of his paternal cousin Nasra, son of Guaram, while Guaram was still alive, in chronicon year 101, during the reign of Guaram;
but Guaram the mampali, his paternal uncle and the father of Nasra, was innocent of the blood of David the curopalates. And this David,
the slain one, left a little son, Adarnase, not yet of age. And Nasr the murderer fled to the empire, to Constantinople, and was there for many years.
And after this they made Gurgen curopalates, the son of Adarnase, son of the great Ashot the curopalates.
Guaram the mampali, son of Ashot the Great and father of Nasr, died in chronicon year 102. And Ashot,
son of Bagrat the curopalates, died in chronicon year 105. And after this Nasr came out of the empire and came to Abkhazia.

And at that time the king of the Abkhaz was Bagrat, Nasr's brother-in-law, and he, the king of the Abkhaz, helped him with a great army; and from there Nasr came down to Samtskhe and gathered another army as well, beyond counting.
But Adarnase, son of the slain curopalates, went out to fight him, and Gurgen the curopalates and his sons went with him to help Adarnase.
And they fought a great battle against Nasr. And God helped these few of Adarnase's party, and they defeated Nasra and put him to flight;
they seized Nasra and killed him in the valley of Samtskhe, at the village of Aspindza, in chronicon year 105. And Nasra left no child, and his memory was blotted out.
Adarnase, son of David the curopalates, was made king of the Georgians in place of his father, who had been killed.
This Adarnase, son of the murdered David, built Bana through Kvirike of Bana, who became the first bishop of Bana.
The mampal Sumbat of Artanuji, son of Adarnase, son of Ashot the Great, died in the koronikon 109. He left two sons: Bagrat, mampal of Artanuji, and David the mampal.
While Sumbat of Artanuji was still alive, Nasr was killed, and these other princes seized Nasr's land.
Gurgen the curopalates left Tao, from Kalmakhi, his own patrimony, to live in Shavsheti and Artani.

After this they became enemies of one another and gathered armies against each other: on one side Gurgen the curopalates and his people, and on the other side Adarnase, king of the Georgians, and Bagrat of Artanuji.
They came to the valley of Artani, to the village of Mglinavi, and fought one another. Gurgen the curopalates was routed. They wounded him and took him captive.
Gurgen the curopalates, son of Adarnase, son of Ashot the Great, died of his wounds in the koronikon 111.
He left two sons: Adarnase and Ashot, the eristavt-eristavi (duke of dukes).
After his father Gurgen the curopalates, Adarnase died in the koronikon 116. He left two young sons:
David the eristavt-eristavi, and Gurgen, who afterwards became the great eristavt-eristavi.
Bagrat, mampal of Artanuji, son of Sumbat, died in the koronikon 129, on the 20th of the month of April, on the day of Mid-Pentecost. He left four sons:
Adarnase, who became a monk and was given the name Basil; Gurgen the eristavi; Ashot; and David.
David the eristavi, son of Adarnase, son of Gurgen the curopalates, and brother of the great Gurgen, died in the koronikon 128 and left no child.
Ashot the eristavt-eristavi, son of Gurgen the curopalates, who was called Kukhi, built Tbeti in Shavsheti and completed it with every provision.
By revelation of the Holy Spirit he installed the blessed Stephen as its first bishop. This Ashot Kukhi died in the koronikon 138 and had no child.
After this, Gurgen, his nephew (his brother's son), son of Adarnase, was made eristavt-eristavi.
David, son of Bagrat of Artanuji, died in the koronikon 142. He left a son in his wife's womb, who was named Bagrat.
Adarnase, king of the Georgians, son of the murdered David, died in the koronikon 143. He left four sons:
David, who became king of the Georgians after his father; Ashot the curopalates; Bagrat the magistros; and Sumbat, who was made curopalates after his brothers.
Gurgen the eristavi, son of Bagrat of Artanuji, died in the koronikon 143, the same year in which Adarnase, king of the Georgians, died.
This Gurgen left a son in his wife's womb, who was also named Gurgen, after his father.
David, king of the Georgians, son of Adarnase, king of the Georgians, died in the koronikon 157 and had no son. Ashot died,
son of Bagrat of Artanuji, in the koronikon 159, in the month of June, and had no son. Gurgen the great eristavt-eristavi, son of Adarnase, died,

who performed greater feats of valour and fought more battles than any of his forefathers, and subjugated all the lands around him, in the koronikon 161, on the 14th of the month of February. He had no son.

Prince (mampali) David, son of Sumbat of Artanuji, died as a monk in the chronicon 113, on the twentieth of the month of February. He left his son Sumbat, who was made duke of dukes (eristavt-eristavi).
Bagrat the magistros, son of Adarnase, king of the Georgians, died in the chronicon 115, in the month of March. He left his son Adarnase,
who became magistros after his father, and became curopalates after his father's brothers.
In the same year that Bagrat the magistros died, Basil the monk of Klarjeti, son of Prince (mampali) Bagrat, died.
Ashot the curopalates, son of Adarnase, king of the Georgians, died in the chronicon 174, and he had no children.
In the same year Ashot, son of Sumbat, died, and he had no son. After Ashot the curopalates, his brother Sumbat was made curopalates.
This Sumbat the curopalates, son of Adarnase, king of the Georgians, died in the chronicon 178, and he left two sons:
Bagrat the duke of dukes, who was made king of the Georgians, the Simple (Regweni), and Adarnase the curopalates.
Adarnase the curopalates, son of Bagrat the magistros, died in the chronicon 181. His sons had seized him and made him a monk.
He died against his will [?], and left sons: Bagrat and David the duke of dukes.
This Bagrat the duke of dukes, son of Adarnase the curopalates, died in the chronicon 186, and his brother David became the great curopalates.
Gurgen, son of Gurgen, son of Prince (mampali) Bagrat, died in the chronicon 188.
Adarnase, son of Sumbat the curopalates and brother of Bagrat the Simple, died in the chronicon 203, and left a son, David the Younger.
Sumbat the duke of dukes of Artanuji, a righteous man, son of Prince (mampali) David, died in the chronicon 208, and left two sons: David and Bagrat.
On the fortieth day after his death his son Bagrat died, and left two sons: Sumbat and Gurgen.
Sumbat, son of Bagrat the Simple, king of the Georgians, died in the chronicon 212, and he had no children.
David, son of Sumbat the glorious duke of dukes, a righteous man, died; and Bagrat the Simple, king of the Georgians, son of the blessed
Sumbat the curopalates, died in the chronicon 214, and left his eldest son Gurgen, who was called king of kings.
This Gurgen had a son, Bagrat, who on his mother's side was the nephew (sister's son) of the kings of the Abkhazians, Demetrius and Theodosius.
Before Gurgen became king, this Bagrat became king in Abkhazia, and for this reason Gurgen was given the title of king of kings.
David the great curopalates, son of Adarnase the curopalates, died in the chronicon 221, and he had no son. And Further Tao was laid waste;
Basil, king of the Greeks, came out, and the nobles (aznaurs) of this David handed the fortresses over to him, and King Basil seized the patrimony of David the curopalates.
Bagrat, king of the Abkhazians, and his father Gurgen went to him.

King Basil gave them honours: the rank of magistros to Gurgen and the rank of curopalates to Bagrat, so that he might somehow make this father and son enemies of each other, and by this device he schemed [?].
But Gurgen was true and righteous, and Basil could not stir up his heart through this treacherous pretext, nor could he succeed by his scheming.
This Gurgen, King of Kings, son of Bagrat, king of the Georgians, died in the koronikon 228. He left behind this son of his, Bagrat, king of the Abkhazians,
the great kouropalates. Bagrat took possession of Tao, his patrimony, and as sole ruler he held all of the Caucasus, from Jiketi as far as Gurgan.
He made Adarbadagan and Shirvan pay him tribute. He ruled Armenia with sovereign power and governed as he wished.
Through his wisdom and his strength he made the king of the Persians his friend and ally, more than his own family had done, and the king of the Greeks also feared him greatly.
This Bagrat the kouropalates summoned the rulers of Klarjeti, Sumbat and Gurgen, sons of Bagrat of Artanuji,
who was the son of his father's sister. They came to pay court to him in the fortress of Panaskerti, and there he seized them.
He took their lands and their fortresses, and he held them as prisoners in the fortress of Tmogvi.
Sumbat of Artanuji died there in the fortress of Tmogvi in the koronikon 231.
In the same way, in that same year Sumbat's brother Gurgen also died, in the koronikon 232. Their children, Sumbat's son Bagrat and Gurgen's son Demetre, went to Constantinople,
to the emperor Basil. The other children of the kings of Klarjeti, who had stayed in their own land, all died in captivity.
After this Bagrat travelled through his whole kingdom: Abkhazia, Hereti and Kakheti. Then he came and spent the winter in the valleys of Tao. When summer came, he came
to that same fortress of Panaskerti in the third year. This Bagrat died there in the koronikon 234, on Friday, the 7th of May.

He left behind his son Giorgi, who became king at the age of 18. When this Giorgi became king, the land of Hereti and Kakheti rebelled against him, and the eristavis there were taken prisoner through the treachery of the nobles.
The lords who had held those lands before took possession of them again.
In the seventh year of this Giorgi's reign, Basil, emperor of the Greeks, marched out against this King Giorgi.
Giorgi went out with a great army, and both sides camped for many days in the land of Basiani.
They did not move to fight each other. Instead Giorgi withdrew, and he came and burned the city of Olti.
From there he came to Kola. The emperor of the Greeks followed his track and pursued him from behind.
When Giorgi's rearguard met Basil's vanguard, a great battle took place in a village called Shirimni.
Many died on both sides, and great eristavis were killed there: Rati son of Liparit, and Khursi.
When King Giorgi heard the sound of the battle, his men became furious. They set out and came to the place where the fighting was, and Emperor Basil also came there with a great army.
The two sides met there, and there was a great battle. Many Greeks died there, both great men and many others.
Giorgi's men carried off the baggage, and the battle grew so fierce that Emperor Basil was about to flee.
But Giorgi's men lost heart: they pulled back and came away. Basil followed them, came to Artaani, and burned it;
he took captive everyone he found. Giorgi went by way of Niali toward Samtskhe, and Basil pursued him from behind by way of Javakheti and laid everything waste.
George crossed over into Trialeti, and Basil also advanced on Trialeti.
And when they drew near each other, George again grew strong in troops, for he had brought the Tsanars and the men of Shaki.
But when Basil saw this, he turned back from Trialeti and went around Javakheti and Artani in the days of winter, and once again laid them waste even worse than before.
And he went and spent the winter in Chaldia, the city of the Trebizondians. And envoys of both these kings went back and forth between them to make a truce and peace.
At this time a great rebellion broke out in Greece [the Byzantine Empire], for Basil's commander-in-chief and Tsarvez joined together,
Tsarvez the son of Phocas the rebel, and Xiphias became king, and they won over to their side all the land of the eastern region. But God honored Basil,
who was greatly afraid, for Xiphias and Tsarvez [?] turned against each other, and all the people who had sided with him were lured into a fortress, seized, and sent to Basil.
And he exiled him to an island and beheaded many of his supporters, among whom was Pheris, son of Jojik, a Georgian.
And King Basil turned back again and came to Basiani. And he demanded fortresses and lands from King George, and promised him a truce and peace.
But King George sent Zviad ahead of himself with a large army. And Zviad made camp on this side of Basiani, [?] as though it were winter.
And King George himself afterwards [?] went out, eager for a truce, with a large and strong army.
But on both sides those treacherous nobles did not allow George to make a truce, for they did not want peace, but urged him to fight.
They incited him against Basil, who supposed that their coming was for a truce and peace, and he supposed this and waited.
But George's men began to fight and routed part of Basil's army.
Then King Basil ordered that their written documents be hung on the tip of a spear, the documents of fidelity and truce that our King George had written to him.
And so King Basil raised them up on the tip of the spear. He held them up to God and said: "Behold, Lord, this writing of theirs and the deed that they are now doing."
And again King Basil took the Wood of Life together with the holy Mandylion, and threw it upon the ground and spoke thus:
"If you give me into the hands of my enemies, I will never again worship you, forever."
And as soon as he had done and said this, at that very moment George's troops who had gone in first were defeated and put to flight;
and the king's Rus detachments came out from the other side, and not one of those who had come first escaped, except a few.
For King George himself and his strongest army had not yet arrived at all, and on that day those of them were killed
who had not wanted to make peace, and all were put to flight. And countless numbers were slain by the edge of the sword, and some fled.
The Greeks carried off a vast amount of booty and the entire royal treasury that he had. And King Basil moved forward a little and pursued from behind.
And again he began to seek a truce and peace as before, for he was afraid of another rebellion in Greece. And they then made peace and concluded a truce.
And King George gave his son Bagrat as a hostage, a three-year-old infant child, and he gave twelve fortresses, and the land that had been held by David the curopalate: Tao, Basiani,
and Javakheti and Shavsheti. And so Basil, king of the Greeks, went away, and he took with him Bagrat, who was a small child.
And he promised George that he would send Bagrat back home after three years.
When the three years had passed, King Basil sent Bagrat, son of George, from the city of Constantinople, as he had promised.
And Bagrat reached Tao and entered his own patrimony at Bana. The katepano of the East escorted him as far as the border of Bagrat's patrimony.
But when that katepano turned back, officials met him with a letter that read: "King Basil, my brother, has died, and I have become king of all Greece.
So now, wherever in the realm George's son Bagrat may have got to, turn him back at once and send him to us."
When the katepano read it, he turned back at once and pursued Bagrat, but he could not catch him,
because Bagrat had already entered his own patrimony and had been strengthened by an army. The katepano was no longer able to fight it, so he turned back and went away.
Behold the great and wonderful mercy of God: how he delivered the righteous one from the hands of his captors and his enemies! This was in the koronikon 245.
And Bagrat came from Greece to his father, King George, and his mother, Queen Mariam, in their city of Kutaisi.
And so they were reunited in peace, and they gave glory and thanks to God for granting them such a blessing.
After this, when two years had passed, George, the father of this Bagrat, died in Trialeti,
at the place called Mqinvarni, in the koronikon 247, on the 16th of August. And they buried him in Kutaisi.
And after him his son Bagrat took the throne as king at nine years of age. But the nobles of Tao went to Greece:
Vache, son of Karichi; John, the bishop of Bana; and with them most of the nobles of Tao, some of whom held fortresses and some of whom did not.
They rebelled against Bagrat and joined Constantine, the brother of Basil, king of the Greeks, who became king after him.
And in the second year King Constantine sent his parakoimomenos with an overwhelming force from his army and countless treasure, far mightier even than King Basil's.
He overran and laid waste the lands that King Basil had laid waste before, and even more.
For he reached Trialeti, below the fortress of Klde-kari, where Bagrat's nobles were at that time. They fought, but not a great deal.
And again nobles rebelled and handed over fortresses. Chanchakhi, the eristavi of Shavsheti, handed over the fortress of Tsepti, and they themselves went off to Greece.
But Saba, the bishop of Mtbevari, built a stronghold near the church of Tbeti and gave it the name Sueti ("the Pillar").
Then he gathered his people, and they went into it: Saba, the bishop of Mtbevari himself, Ezra, the bishop of Ancha, and the nobles of Shavsheti. And they made themselves strong inside it.
But the parakoimomenos sent John the chartoularios, called Valang, there with a very large army,
and he sent with him Demetre, son of Gurgen of Klarjeti, to win over the inhabitants of the land, and that is what happened.
For the people, the villages, who were foolish and weak in understanding and judgement, went over to them.
And they set their armies against the tower of Tbeti and fought fiercely, with all their might.
And God strengthened those who were inside the tower, through the grace and intercession of the holy apostles and through the prayers of these holy bishops.
And like faithful and true martyrs of God, they gave themselves up to death,
and they gave themselves up for their earthly lords, and shed their blood according to the word of the apostles, and grew strong.
They all said to one another: "Let these flatteries and swiftly passing riches not deceive us; rather, let us win the grace of loyalty and the crown of valor."
For the fighters besieging them flattered them with promises and fair announcements, and with offers of riches.
But while the East was being tormented in this way, as if by a wave that had risen up, wrath swiftly overtook that unjust king Constantine,
just as it overtook Julian the lawless, because of his mercilessness toward our king Bagrat and because he devastated Bagrat's patrimony.
And he quickly wrote to Parkimanos, his proedros, that he should return at once with his army and come to Constantinople.
And when he heard this, he departed. And when this king Constantine died, he left the kingship after him to Romanos, his kinsman and close associate.
After this, in the third year, the blessed queen Mariam, mother of king Bagrat, put on courage and valor,
for she was descended from those illustrious, mighty and great Arshakuni kings. And she went to Constantinople, before king Romanos,
to beg him to make peace for the East, so that there would be no more war between the Greeks and the Georgians,
and so that the poor might be calm and at peace, and so that he would grant her son, king Bagrat, an honor according to the custom of [court] titles.
